Do you want this guy rolling around your home? Maybe if it does laundry… Weave Robotics, a San Francisco startup backed by Y Combinator, has launched Isaac 1, a home robot designed to tackle laundry and light tidying. Rather than following the humanoid trend, Isaac 1 uses a wheeled base and extends from three feet to five foot nine depending on the task, with two articulated arms offering an 80-inch vertical reach.  It's built to autonomously locate dirty clothes, manage hampers, and fold garments, though human teleoperators can step in remotely when it gets stuck. And yes, that means someone may occasionally see inside your home through its cameras.  Priced at $7,999 upfront or $449 a month, it undercuts 1X's Neo by more than half. California deliveries begin this fall. #fyp #robot #techtok

China's LIFELIKE Robot Face Will Make You Question Everything #news #technology #china #robot  Chinese startup AheadForm has built a humanoid robot head that is nearly impossible to distinguish from a real human face. Powered by thirty precision brushless micro motors embedded beneath bionic silicone skin, the robot controls every blink, every glance, and every subtle micro expression with stunning accuracy. Cameras integrated directly into the eyes allow the robot to track faces in real time, while an onboard AI system reads human emotions and responds instantly with matching expressions. This is not a CGI render or a movie prop. This is real technology being developed right now in China for deployment in customer service, healthcare, and personal companionship. A viral video of the robot posted in March 2026 reignited a global conversation about whether hyper realistic robot faces are the missing key to making humanoid robots commercially successful. AheadForm believes the future of human robot interaction depends not just on what robots can do, but on how real they feel. The face of the future just got a lot harder to spot.

You can now buy a humanoid robot for $4K Humanoid robots just got insanely cheap, and this might change everything. In this video, we break down how Unitree Robotics just launched a $4,000 humanoid robot on AliExpress, a price point that was unthinkable just a few years ago. The R1 robot stands 123cm tall and can perform advanced movements like cartwheels, running downhill, and getting back up on its own. What’s wild? Robots with similar capabilities used to cost anywhere from $50,000 to $150,000, meaning prices have dropped by over 90%. Even more surprising, China is already dominating the humanoid robotics race. While companies like Tesla, Figure AI, and Agility Robotics have only shipped around 150 units each, Unitree has already shipped over 5,500 robots. What used to live in research labs and sci-fi movies is now available to anyone with a credit card, on the same platform you would use to buy everyday gadgets. So the real question is what happens when humanoid robots become this affordable? Drop your thoughts in the comments and subscribe for more content on the future of tech, AI, and innovation.

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

Clone Robotics just dropped new footage of Torso 3 under teleoperation. And this robot still looks like something pulled straight out of a sci-fi lab. Torso 3 uses Clone’s musculoskeletal approach, with artificial muscles attached around a human-like skeleton instead of conventional motor-driven joints. In the new footage, the robot is suspended from above while the operator controls its movements. You can see the shoulders, arms, torso, hips, legs and hands moving together through large ranges of motion. One technical update on Torso 3 is joint-angle feedback in the hands. Clone has also moved its valves in-house, bringing more of the muscle control hardware inside the robot itself. My eyes keep going back to the hands. Finger movement is one of the hardest parts of humanoid control, and knowing the actual joint angles gives the controller direct feedback about where each joint moved after the muscles were commanded. The overhead support is also a reminder of where the system is today. This clip shows teleoperated full-body motion. It does not show autonomous walking or unsupported balance yet. Clone is taking a very different mechanical route from humanoids built around electric motors and gearboxes. Human-like bones, artificial muscles and fluid control make the machine move in a way that is instantly recognizable. Torso 3 is getting closer to looking like a synthetic body under active control. Would you feel comfortable standing next to this robot? #CloneRobotics #HumanoidRobot #Robotics #PhysicalAI #EmbodiedAI

The gap between factory-built robots and DIY projects is getting smaller. Look at these two machines. The top clip shows Galileo, a four-wheeled robot with articulated legs. The robot below is a DIY build made with patched-together parts. I watched the lower clip twice. Its metal frame is exposed and the parts look like they came from different projects. Yet all four wheels move on articulated supports. Pretty impressive for a homemade machine. Motors, controllers, batteries and metal parts are now easier for individual builders to buy and assemble without owning a factory. This short video doesn't prove the DIY robot can match Galileo's performance. We have no figures for payload, accuracy, reliability or lifespan. Factories still do work that's hard to reproduce at home. They machine parts to tight tolerances, inspect assemblies, test safety and produce hundreds or thousands of identical units. But I keep thinking about that bottom robot. Someone assembled a moving four-wheeled machine using improvised parts. That alone would have been a difficult project for most hobbyists years ago. As parts and tools become easier to get, more people can build machines that once seemed out of reach. What happens to assembly factories when complex robots become easier to make at home? Will they focus on precision parts, testing and large-scale production while more assembly moves to small workshops? #Robotics #DIYRobotics #Manufacturing #PhysicalAI
